NewsContent:
​“Urinary Incontinence (UI) is the complaint of any involuntary leakage of urine which affects 3 in 10 women worldwide,” prominent gynaecologist Dr Raheela Mohsin informed the audience at Aga Khan University’s (AKU) ‘Sign, Symptoms and Care’ public health awareness programme held at AKU .​

Dr Raheela Mohsin who is Assistant Professor, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at AKU, pointed out that although UI is very common among female population, it is believed to be considerably underreported because of cultural sensitivities and the stigma attached to urinary incontinence. UI is not a life –threatening disease but the symptoms may seriously influence the physical, psychological and social well being of affected individuals.

The overall prevalence ranges from 53% among Asian females and 22% among European females.

Urinary incontinence occurs when the sphincter muscles at the base of bladder fail to hold back the flow of urine. In healthy people these sphincter muscles remain rigid until the urge to urinate becomes too strong to ignore.

Urinary incontinence is a symptom of lower urinary tract disorder, but it is only one among several significant urinary symptoms. People suffering from incontinence, may not be able to void (empty) all of their urine in one sitting, leaving some in bladder. This may signal the sphincter muscles to relax involuntarily, causing a urinary leak.

The other common types of urinary incontinence are: (a)Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) which is the most common type of incontinence and is due to changes resulting from pregnancy, childbirth, and menopause; (b)Urge urinary incontinence (UUI) is the complaint of involuntary leakage accompanied by or immediately preceded by urgency. (c) Mixed urinary incontinence (MUI) is a combination of stress and urge UI. Usually one type is more bothersome than the other is. The cause of two forms may or may not be related.

In most cases, a preliminary diagnosis of urinary incontinence can be made and treatment initiated based on findings of the medical history, physical examination and simple laboratory testing.

Strategies for treatment of stress incontinence include pelvic floor rehabilitation, occlusive devices, medication and surgery while estrogen replacement therapy is effective against both stress and urge urinary incontinence.

Although common Urinary incontinence isn’t necessarily a part of aging, it is a medical condition which in most cases can be eliminated and modern products and ways of managing UI can ease the discomfort and inconvenience. The screening and diagnosis is always possible provided if people see their physician for complete medical examination and report their urinary symptoms. Continence promotion programmes are required to break the cultural barriers.

In the same programme, Dr Samina Ismail, Consultant Anaesthetist and Assistant Professor, Department of Anaesthesia, spoke to the audience about options of pain management in labour.

She said that modern obstetrical anaesthesia offers mothers a variety of safe choices for increasing patient comfort during labour. Many women experience significant pain during labour and choose to use pain medication.

There are number of methods available for pain relief like narcotics, nitrous oxide, patient controlled narcotic analgesia and regional anaesthesia (epidural anaesthesia.) Among the method of pain relief epidural is the most effective and widely accepted method of pain relief for labour and birth. Dr Ismail discussed different options for pain relief for labour pain with detailed information about epidural.

As part of its outreach programme and societal commitment to create awareness of early diagnosis and timely treatment, AKUH has organised over 200 ‘Signs, Symptoms and Care’ programmes in Karachi, Hyderabad and the UAE, benefiting more than 40,000 people. Similarly, Aga Khan University Hospital’s Patient Welfare Programme offers financial assistance to those patients who are unable to afford the medical cost of treatment. In 2004, 74 per cent of all patients treated at AKUH were from low- to middle-income groups. Since the inception of this welfare programme in 1986, over Rs 1.4 billion has been disbursed to more than 250,000 needy patients.
